fact: A CLASS DIAGRAM depicts the object structure of a system, showing the classes, their attributes and operations, and the relationships between them
A class is drawn as a rectangle divided into THREE COMPARTMENTS: the class NAME at the top, its ATTRIBUTES in the middle, and its OPERATIONS at the bottom

ASSOCIATION is a general relationship between two classes showing that objects of one are connected to objects of another; it is drawn as a line often labelled with the MULTIPLICITY, such as 1 or M, for example one Student associated with many Enrolment records

AGGREGATION is a special form of association representing a WHOLE-PART relationship where the part CAN exist independently of the whole; for example a Department has Lecturers, but a lecturer can transfer to another department and continue to exist

COMPOSITION is a STRONGER form of aggregation where the part CANNOT exist without the whole; for example an Order is made up of Order Lines, and if the order is deleted its order lines are deleted with it

INHERITANCE or generalisation is a relationship where a SUBCLASS is a specialised version of a SUPERCLASS and inherits its attributes and operations; it is drawn as a line with a HOLLOW TRIANGLE pointing to the superclass
The four class relationships look similar because a line is a line; the small SYMBOL at one end of the line is what tells them apart

The FIVE steps to build a class diagram are: identify the candidate classes from the requirements model, particularly the use case diagram and narratives; identify the relationships and multiplicity between classes; identify the attributes of each class; identify the operations of each class; and check that the classes are consistent with the use cases already produced

In the worked class diagram, Student and Course are the two main classes and ENROLMENT is the ASSOCIATIVE CLASS needed because a student can register for many courses and a course can have many students
Although use case diagrams were introduced as part of requirements modelling, they are also considered a UML BEHAVIOURAL diagram, since they depict how external agents interact with the system
INCLUDE means a base use case ALWAYS requires the behaviour of another use case to complete, for example Record Grades includes Save Grades since every act of recording must end with saving
EXTEND means a use case OPTIONALLY adds extra behaviour to a base use case under certain conditions, for example Place Order extended by Apply Discount but only when a discount code is entered
Include and extend are easy to confuse because BOTH are drawn as DASHED ARROWS; the direction of the arrow and the everyday meaning of ALWAYS against SOMETIMES is what distinguishes them

The FOUR steps to build a use case diagram are: identify the actors, the people or external systems that will use the system; identify the use cases, the tasks each actor needs to perform; draw an association line from each actor to every use case they are involved in; and identify any include or extend relationships between use cases, drawn as dashed arrows labelled accordingly

In the school grading worked example the actors are Teacher, Administrator and Student; the use cases are Record Grades, Update Grades, Distribute Report Cards, Generate Report Cards and View Grades; Record Grades and Update Grades both include a Save/Load Grades use case, and View Grades includes a Login use case
